core_summary: Focuses on advanced statistical aggregation and multi-category data visualization. Explains why simple arithmetic averages fail when combining groups of unequal size or items with different weights, necessitating the weighted arithmetic mean formula. Introduces cluster-column graphs, stacked bar charts, and 100% stacked bar charts for multi-variable data representation, demonstrating how normalizing bars to 100% isolates relative percentage allocations regardless of total group magnitudes.
key_concepts: Fallacy of Unweighted Group Averages (simple average of subgroup averages distorts overall mean when group sizes differ)
Weighted Arithmetic Mean (multiplying subgroup values by their respective weights/counts)
Weight Factors in Assessment and Mixing (assigning relative importance ratios in academic grading or alloy mixtures)
Data Visualization for Multi-Category Sets (representing multiple categorical variables simultaneously)
Cluster-Column Charts (placing category bars side by side for direct absolute comparison)
Standard Stacked Bar Charts (stacking category values to preserve absolute total height alongside components)
100% Stacked Bar Charts (scaling all stacked bars to 100% to compare relative component percentages across different group sizes)
Mixture and Concentration Aggregation (calculating combined percentage concentration when mixing batches of different volumes)
Conservation of Total Mass/Value in Combined Averages (ensuring total combined sum equals sum of component weighted products)

key_terms.definition: An average where each data point is multiplied by a weight reflecting its relative frequency, size, or importance.
A numerical value representing the count, volume, or relative importance of a data component.
The sum of values divided by the number of values, valid only when all components have equal weight.
A chart featuring grouped vertical bars comparing distinct categories side by side.
A chart where visual bars are divided into sub-segments representing individual category components, showing totals.
A bar chart normalized to 100% height, displaying relative percentage contributions of each category.
The process of combining statistics from distinct sub-populations into a single composite metric.
The proportion of a specific substance relative to the total mass or volume of a mixture.

key_takeaways: Never take a simple average of averages unless all groups have identical sample sizes.
The weighted mean formula x_bar = sum(w_i * x_i) / sum(w_i) accurately accounts for unequal sample sizes and component weights.
Use standard stacked bar charts to compare absolute totals; use 100% stacked bar charts to compare relative budget allocations or proportions.
Percentage concentrations in mixtures follow weighted average principles based on batch masses or volumes.
subject: Maths II
